Nociceptor

Protein kinase A, activated by the β2 receptor's own Gs signal, phosphorylates the receptor and shifts its coupling from Gs to Gi. In nociceptors this switch is seen after stress, when adrenaline produces a longer-lasting hyperalgesia through Gi and Gβγ signalling. It is one way stress may worsen chronic joint pain.

Spinal nociceptive neuron

In cell lines, protein kinase A phosphorylates the β2 receptor and switches its coupling from Gs to Gi. Whether this happens in dorsal horn neurons is not known.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Metabolites take a lighter shade of the same colour. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Noradrenaline and the β2 receptor are red: in nociceptors the switch of β2 to Gi after stress prolongs hyperalgesia. In dorsal horn neurons the switch is not known, and so neither is its effect on pain.
